annotations.text:
Four directions, same feed, same real listings - so you are comparing treatment, not copy.
Each row is one direction: web on the left, Android on the right.
Pick a row. Each artboard has an accent-colour chip above it if you want to try a different hue before deciding.

MARKET STALL
Warm paper, ink, one persimmon accent. Instrument Serif for titles and prices, near-square corners, hairline rules, no shadows.

Why: reads like a local classifieds page. Human and trustworthy - it looks like neighbours, not a platform.

Tradeoff: the least app-like of the four. Serif at small sizes needs care, and it can feel slow next to a dense utility UI.

SIGNAL
Pure white and black, one electric blue, 2px borders, hard offset shadows, zero radius. Archivo Black headlines, JetBrains Mono for every number.

Why: unmistakable and fast. Prices and distances read instantly because the mono numerals line up.

Tradeoff: loud and a bit cold. Brutalism dates faster than the other three, and the heavy borders eat space on a phone.

NIGHTFALL
Deep blue-black, mint and periwinkle accents, 16px radii, the radius ring as the hero surface with price pins on it.

Why: makes the actual product idea - a distance ring around you - the thing you see first. Looks the most premium.

Tradeoff: dark UI is harder for outdoor daytime use, photos of second-hand junk look worse on dark, and it needs real map tiles to pay off.

POCKET
Soft lilac ground, white cards, 22px radii, a pastel colour per category, a floating pill nav. Outfit throughout.

Why: lowest barrier of the four - the category colours do the sorting for you, and it invites casual listing.

Tradeoff: the friendliest and the least serious. Once real money and deposits are on screen in Phase 5, soft and round can undercut trust.

LEDGER
Swiss and data-first: a real table, IBM Plex Sans and Mono, hairline rules, a facet rail instead of chips. No photos at all.

Why: the fastest thing to scan. Tabular numerals mean prices and distances line up down the column, so comparing 12 listings takes one pass.

Tradeoff: cold and expert-feeling. A ladder is a physical object and this shows you none of it.

POSTCARD
Photo-first magazine: full-bleed image tiles, an asymmetric mosaic, Bodoni Moda at display size with text laid over the image.

Why: makes the stuff look worth having, and rewards idle browsing rather than targeted searching.

Tradeoff: it lives or dies on photo quality - and these are phone snaps of a drill in a cellar. Lowest information density of all nine.

TERMINAL
Amber on black, IBM Plex Mono throughout, a command prompt as the search bar, results as numbered rows, keyboard hints along the bottom.

Why: nobody forgets it. Genuinely the fastest to read once learned, and tiny to render.

Tradeoff: the honest one - this is a costume. Your audience is neighbours borrowing ladders, and a fake shell will read as unwelcoming to most of them.

BLOOM
Warm stone ground with soft colour washes, Newsreader italic for headlines, organic petal-shaped image masks, sage and clay accents.

Why: calm and grown-up warmth. Gets the approachability of Pocket without the toy feeling, which matters once deposits are on screen.

Tradeoff: the soft shapes and low contrast need care to stay accessible, and it is the least distinctive at a glance.

TRANSIT
Wayfinding: a coloured line per category, listings as stops down a route, distance set large as the primary label, signage-grade contrast.

Why: the strongest idea of the nine - it makes distance the structure rather than a footnote, which is exactly what Radius is about.

Tradeoff: a strong metaphor fights unusual content. A route implies order and direction that a feed does not really have.
